changed the human lifestyle. Agriculture began independently in different parts of the globe, and included a diverse
range of <color=#3366CC>taxa</color>, in at least 11 separate centers of origin. <color=#3366CC>Cereal crop</color> cultivation and animal domestication had occurred
in <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color> by at least 8500 BCE in the form of wheat, <color=#3366CC>barley</color>, sheep, and goats. The <color=#3366CC>Yangtze River Valley</color> in
China domesticated rice around 8000–7000 BCE; the <color=#3366CC>Yellow River Valley</color> may have cultivated <color=#3366CC>millet</color> by 7000 BCE.
Pigs were the most important domesticated animal in early China. People in Africa's <color=#3366CC>Sahara</color> cultivated <color=#3366CC>sorghum</color> and
several other crops between 8000 and 5000 BCE, while other agricultural centers arose in the <color=#3366CC>Ethiopian Highlands</color> and
the West African rainforests. In the <color=#3366CC>Indus River Valley</color>, crops were cultivated by 7000 BCE, and cattle were
domesticated by 6500 BCE. In the Americas, <color=#3366CC>squash</color> was cultivated by at least 8500 BCE in South America, and
domesticated <color=#3366CC>arrowroot</color> appeared in Central America by 7800 BCE. Potatoes were first cultivated in the <color=#3366CC>Andes</color> of South
America, where the <color=#3366CC>llama</color> was also domesticated. It is likely that women played a central role in plant domestication
throughout these developments.
Various explanations of the causes of the Neolithic Revolution have been proposed. Some theories identify population
growth as the main factor, leading people to seek out new food sources. Others see population growth not as the cause
but as the effect of the associated improvements in food supply. Further suggested factors include climate change,
resource scarcity, and ideology. The transition to agriculture created food surpluses that could support people not
directly engaged in food production, permitting far denser populations and the creation of the first cities and <color=#3366CC>states</color>.
Cities were centers of <color=#3366CC>trade</color>, <color=#3366CC>manufacturing</color>, and <color=#3366CC>political power</color>. They developed mutually beneficial relationships with
the inhabitants of the surrounding <color=#3366CC>countrysides</color>, receiving agricultural products and providing manufactured goods and
varying degrees of political control in return. Pastoral societies based on nomadic animal herding also developed,
mostly in dry areas unsuited to plant cultivation, such as the <color=#3366CC>Eurasian Steppe</color> and the African <color=#3366CC>Sahel</color>. Conflict between
nomadic herders and sedentary agriculturalists was frequent and became a recurring theme in world history.
<color=#3366CC>Metalworking</color> was first used in the creation of copper tools and ornaments around 6400 BCE. Gold and silver soon
followed, primarily for use in ornaments. The first signs of <color=#3366CC>bronze</color>, an alloy of copper and <color=#3366CC>tin</color>, date to around 4500 BCE,
but the alloy was not widely used until the 3rd millennium BCE.
Ancient
Cradles of civilization
The Bronze Age saw the development of cities and <color=#3366CC>civilizations</color>. Early civilizations arose close to rivers, first in
Mesopotamia (3300 BCE) along the Tigris and Euphrates, followed by the <color=#3366CC>Egyptian civilization</color> along the <color=#3366CC>Nile River</color>
(3200 BCE), the <color=#3366CC>Norte Chico civilization</color> in coastal <color=#3366CC>Peru</color> (3100 BCE), the <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley Civilization</color> in Pakistan and
northwestern India (2500 BCE), and the <color=#3366CC>Chinese civilization</color> along the <color=#3366CC>Yangtze</color> and <color=#3366CC>Yellow Rivers</color> (2200 BCE).
These societies developed a number of shared characteristics, including a central government, a complex economy
and social structure, and systems for keeping records. These cultures variously invented the <color=#3366CC>wheel</color>, <color=#3366CC>mathematics</color>,
bronze-working, sailing boats, the <color=#3366CC>potter's wheel</color>, <color=#3366CC>woven</color> cloth, construction of monumental buildings, and <color=#3366CC>writing</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Polytheistic</color> religions developed, centered on temples where <color=#3366CC>priests</color> and priestesses performed <color=#3366CC>sacrificial</color> rites.
Writing facilitated the administration of cities, the expression of ideas, and the preservation of information. It may have
independently developed in at least four ancient civilizations: Mesopotamia (3300 BCE), Egypt (around 3250 BCE),
China (1200 BCE), and lowland <color=#3366CC>Mesoamerica</color> (by 650 BCE). The earliest system of writing was the Mesopotamian
<color=#3366CC>cuneiform script</color>, which began as a system of <color=#3366CC>pictographs</color>, whose pictorial representations eventually became simplified
and more abstract. Other influential early writing systems include <color=#3366CC>Egyptian hieroglyphs</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Indus script</color>. In China,
writing was first used during the <color=#3366CC>Shang dynasty</color> (1766–1045 BCE).
Transport was facilitated by waterways, including rivers and seas, which fostered the projection of military power and
the exchange of goods, ideas, and inventions. The Bronze Age also saw new land technologies, such as horse-based
<color=#3366CC>cavalry</color> and <color=#3366CC>chariots</color>, that allowed <color=#3366CC>armies</color> to move faster. Trade became increasingly important as urban societies
exchanged manufactured goods for raw materials from distant lands, creating vast commercial networks and the
beginnings of archaic globalization. Bronze production in Southwest Asia, for example, required the import of tin from
as far away as England.
The growth of cities was often followed by the establishment of states and empires. In Egypt, the initial division into
Upper and Lower Egypt was followed by the unification of the whole valley around 3100 BCE. Around 2600 BCE, the
Indus Valley civilization built major cities at <color=#3366CC>Harappa</color> and <color=#3366CC>Mohenjo-daro</color>. Mesopotamian history was characterized by
frequent wars between city-states, leading to shifts in <color=#3366CC>hegemony</color> from one city to another. In the 25th–21st centuries
BCE, the empires of <color=#3366CC>Akkad</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Neo-Sumerians</color> arose in this area. In Crete, the <color=#3366CC>Minoan civilization</color> emerged by
2000 BCE and is regarded as the first civilization in Europe.
Over the following millennia, civilizations developed across the world. By 1600 BCE, <color=#3366CC>Mycenaean Greece</color> began to
develop. It flourished until the <color=#3366CC>Late Bronze Age collapse</color> that affected many Mediterranean civilizations between 1300
and 1000 BCE. The foundations of many cultural aspects in India were laid in the <color=#3366CC>Vedic period</color> (1750–600 BCE),
including the emergence of <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>. From around 550 BCE, many independent kingdoms and republics known as the
<color=#3366CC>Mahajanapadas</color> were established across the subcontinent.
Speakers of the <color=#3366CC>Bantu languages</color> began <color=#3366CC>expanding</color> across Central, Eastern, and Southern Africa as early as 3000 BCE
until 1000 CE. Their expansion and encounters with other groups resulted in the displacement of the <color=#3366CC>Pygmy peoples</color>
and the Khoisan, and in the spread of mixed farming and ironworking throughout sub-Saharan Africa, laying the
foundations for later states.
The <color=#3366CC>Lapita culture</color> emerged in the <color=#3366CC>Bismarck Archipelago</color> near <color=#3366CC>New Guinea</color> around 1500 BCE and colonized many
uninhabited islands of Remote Oceania, reaching as far as <color=#3366CC>Samoa</color> by 700 BCE.
In the Americas, the Norte Chico culture emerged in Peru around 3100 BCE. The Norte Chico built public monumental
architecture at the city of <color=#3366CC>Caral</color>, dated 2627–1977 BCE. The later <color=#3366CC>Chavín</color> polity is sometimes described as the first
<color=#3366CC>Andean</color> state, centered on the religious site at Chavín de Huántar. Other important Andean cultures include the <color=#3366CC>Moche</color>,
whose ceramics depict many aspects of daily life, and the <color=#3366CC>Nazca</color>, who created animal-shaped designs in the desert
called <color=#3366CC>Nazca lines</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Olmecs</color> of Mesoamerica developed by about 1200 BCE and are known for the <color=#3366CC>colossal stone</color>
<color=#3366CC>heads</color> that they carved from <color=#3366CC>basalt</color>. They also devised the Mesoamerican calendar that was used by later cultures such
as the <color=#3366CC>Maya</color> and <color=#3366CC>Teotihuacan</color>. Societies in North America were primarily egalitarian hunter-gatherers, supplementing
their diet with the plants of the Eastern Agricultural Complex. They built earthworks such as Watson Brake (4000 BCE)
and Poverty Point (3600 BCE), both in Louisiana.
Axial Age
From 800 to 200 BCE, the Axial Age saw the emergence of transformative philosophical and religious ideas that
developed in many different places mostly independently of each other. Chinese <color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color>, Indian <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Jainism</color>, and Jewish <color=#3366CC>monotheism</color> all arose during this period. Persian <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrianism</color> began earlier, perhaps around
1000 BCE, but was institutionalized by the <color=#3366CC>Achaemenid Empire</color> during the Axial Age. <color=#3366CC>New philosophies</color> took hold in
Greece during the 5th century BCE, epitomized by thinkers such as <color=#3366CC>Plato</color> and <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>. The first <color=#3366CC>Olympic Games</color> were
held in 776 BCE, marking a period known as "<color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color>". In 508 BCE, <color=#3366CC>the world's first democratic system</color> of
government was instituted in <color=#3366CC>Athens</color>.
Axial Age ideas shaped subsequent intellectual and religious history. Confucianism was one of the three schools of
thought that came to dominate Chinese thinking, along with <color=#3366CC>Taoism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Legalism</color>. The Confucian tradition, which
would become particularly influential, looked for political morality not to the force of law but to the power and example of
tradition. Confucianism would later spread to <color=#3366CC>Korea</color> and Japan. Buddhism reached China in about the 1st century CE
and spread widely, with 30,000 Buddhist temples in northern China alone by the 7th century CE. Buddhism became the
main religion in much of South, Southeast, and East Asia. The Greek philosophical tradition diffused throughout the
Mediterranean world and as far as India, starting in the 4th century BCE after the conquests of <color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color> of
<color=#3366CC>Macedon</color>. Both <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> and <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> developed from the beliefs of <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>.
Regional empires
The millennium from 500 BCE to 500 CE saw a series of empires of unprecedented size develop. Well-trained
professional armies, unifying ideologies, and advanced bureaucracies created the possibility for emperors to rule over
large domains whose populations could attain numbers upwards of tens of millions of subjects. <color=#3366CC>International trade</color> also
expanded, most notably the massive trade routes in the Mediterranean Sea, the <color=#3366CC>maritime trade web in the Indian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Ocean</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Silk Road</color>.
The kingdom of the <color=#3366CC>Medes</color> helped to destroy the <color=#3366CC>Assyrian Empire</color> in tandem with the nomadic <color=#3366CC>Scythians</color> and the
<color=#3366CC>Babylonians</color>. <color=#3366CC>Nineveh</color>, the capital of Assyria, was sacked by the Medes in 612 BCE. The Median Empire gave way to

successive <color=#3366CC>Iranian</color> states, including the <color=#3366CC>Achaemenid</color> (550–330 BCE), <color=#3366CC>Parthian</color> (247 BCE – 224 CE), and <color=#3366CC>Sasanian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empires</color> (224–651 CE).
Two major empires began in modern-day <color=#3366CC>Greece</color>. In the late 5th century BCE, several Greek <color=#3366CC>city-states</color> checked the
Achaemenid Persian advance in Europe through the <color=#3366CC>Greco-Persian Wars</color>. These wars were followed by the Golden
Age of Athens, the seminal period of ancient Greece that laid many of the foundations of <color=#3366CC>Western civilization</color>, including
the <color=#3366CC>first theatrical performances</color>. The wars led to the creation of the <color=#3366CC>Delian League</color>, founded in 477 BCE, and
eventually the <color=#3366CC>Athenian Empire</color> (454–404 BCE), which was defeated by a Spartan-led coalition during the
<color=#3366CC>Peloponnesian War</color>. <color=#3366CC>Philip of Macedon</color> unified the Greek city-states into the <color=#3366CC>Hellenic League</color>, and his son Alexander
the Great (356–323 BCE) founded an empire extending from present-day Greece to India. The empire divided into
several <color=#3366CC>successor states</color> shortly after his death, resulting in the founding of many cities and the spread of Greek culture
throughout conquered regions, a process referred to as Hellenization. The <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic period</color> lasted from the death of
Alexander in 323 BCE until 31 BCE, when <color=#3366CC>Ptolemaic Egypt</color> fell to Rome.
In Europe, the <color=#3366CC>Roman Republic</color> was founded in the 6th century BCE and began expanding its territory in the 3rd
century BCE. Prior to this, the <color=#3366CC>Carthaginian Empire</color> had dominated the Mediterranean; however, it lost <color=#3366CC>three successive</color>
<color=#3366CC>wars</color> to the Romans. The Republic became <color=#3366CC>an empire</color>, and by the time of <color=#3366CC>Augustus</color> (63 BCE – 14 CE), it had
established dominion over most of the Mediterranean Sea. The empire continued to grow and reached its peak under
<color=#3366CC>Trajan</color> (53–117 CE), controlling much of the land from England to Mesopotamia. The two centuries that followed are
known as the <color=#3366CC>Pax Romana</color>, a period of unprecedented peace, prosperity, and political stability in most of Europe.
Christianity was <color=#3366CC>legalized</color> by <color=#3366CC>Constantine I</color> in 313 CE after three centuries of imperial persecution. It became the sole
official religion of the empire in 380 CE while the emperor <color=#3366CC>Theodosius</color> outlawed <color=#3366CC>pagan religions</color> in 391–392 CE.
In South Asia, <color=#3366CC>Chandragupta Maurya</color> founded the <color=#3366CC>Maurya Empire</color> (320–185 BCE), which flourished under <color=#3366CC>Ashoka the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Great</color>. From the 4th to 6th centuries CE, the <color=#3366CC>Gupta Empire</color> oversaw the period referred to as ancient India's golden
age. The resulting stability helped usher in a flourishing period for Hindu and Buddhist culture in the 4th and 5th
centuries, as well as major advances in science and mathematics. In <color=#3366CC>South India</color>, three prominent <color=#3366CC>Dravidian</color> kingdoms
emerged: the <color=#3366CC>Cheras</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cholas</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Pandyas</color>.
In China, <color=#3366CC>Qin Shi Huang</color> put an end to the chaotic <color=#3366CC>Warring States period</color> by uniting all of China under the <color=#3366CC>Qin dynasty</color>
(221–206 BCE). Qin Shi Huang was an adherent of the Legalist school of thought, and he displaced the hereditary
aristocracy by creating an efficient system of administration staffed by officials appointed according to merit. The
harshness of the Qin dynasty led to rebellions and the dynasty's fall. It was followed by the <color=#3366CC>Han dynasty</color> (202 BCE –
220 CE), which combined the Legalist bureaucratic system with Confucian ideals. The Han dynasty was comparable in
power and influence to the Roman Empire that lay at the other end of the Silk Road. As economic prosperity fueled
their military expansion, the Han conquered parts of Mongolia, Central Asia, <color=#3366CC>Manchuria</color>, Korea, and northern Vietnam.
As with other empires during the classical period, Han China advanced significantly in the areas of government,
education, science, and technology. The Han invented the <color=#3366CC>compass</color>, one of China's Four Great Inventions.
In Africa, the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Kush</color> prospered through its interactions with both Egypt and sub-Saharan Africa. It ruled
Egypt as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty from 712 to 650 BCE, then continued as an agricultural and trading state based in
the city of <color=#3366CC>Meroë</color> until the fourth century CE. The <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Aksum</color>, centered in present-day Ethiopia, established
itself by the 1st century CE as a major trading empire, dominating its neighbors in <color=#3366CC>South Arabia</color> and Kush and
controlling the <color=#3366CC>Red Sea</color> trade. It minted its own currency and carved enormous monolithic stelae to mark its emperors'
graves.
Successful regional empires were also established in the Americas, arising from cultures established as early as 2500
BCE. In Mesoamerica, vast <color=#3366CC>pre-Columbian</color> societies were built, the most notable being the <color=#3366CC>Zapotec civilization</color> (700
BCE – 1521 CE), and the <color=#3366CC>Maya civilization</color>, which reached its highest state of development during the Mesoamerican
classic period (c. 250–900 CE), but continued throughout the post-classic period. The great Maya <color=#3366CC>city-states</color> slowly
rose in number and prominence, and Maya culture spread throughout the <color=#3366CC>Yucatán</color> and surrounding areas. The Maya
developed <color=#3366CC>a writing system</color> and used the concept of zero in their mathematics. West of the Maya area, in central
Mexico, the city of <color=#3366CC>Teotihuacan</color> prospered due to its control of the <color=#3366CC>obsidian</color> trade. Its power peaked around 450 CE,
when its 125,000–150,000 inhabitants made it one of the world's largest cities.
<color=#3366CC>Technology developed sporadically</color> in the ancient world. There were periods of rapid technological progress, such as
the Greco-Roman era in the Mediterranean region. <color=#3366CC>Greek science</color>, <color=#3366CC>technology</color>, and mathematics are generally
considered to have reached their peak during the Hellenistic period, typified by devices such as the <color=#3366CC>Antikythera</color>
<color=#3366CC>mechanism</color>. There were also periods of technological decay, such as the Roman Empire's decline and fall and the
ensuing early medieval period. Two of the most important innovations were paper (China, 1st and 2nd centuries CE)
and the <color=#3366CC>stirrup</color> (India, 2nd century BCE and Central Asia, 1st century CE), both of which diffused widely throughout the
world. The Chinese learned to make silk and built massive engineering projects such as the <color=#3366CC>Great Wall of China</color> and
the <color=#3366CC>Grand Canal</color>. The Romans were also accomplished builders, inventing <color=#3366CC>concrete</color>, perfecting the use of <color=#3366CC>arches</color> in
construction, and creating aqueducts to transport water over long distances to urban centers.
Most ancient societies practiced <color=#3366CC>slavery</color>, which was particularly prevalent in Athens and Rome, where slaves made up
a large proportion of the population and were foundational to the economy. <color=#3366CC>Patriarchy</color> was also common, with men
controlling more political and economic power than women.
Declines, falls, and resurgence
The ancient empires faced common problems associated with maintaining huge armies and supporting a central
<color=#3366CC>bureaucracy</color>. In Rome and Han China, the state began to decline, and <color=#3366CC>barbarian</color> pressure on the frontiers hastened
internal dissolution. The Han dynasty fell into civil war in 220 CE, beginning the <color=#3366CC>Three Kingdoms</color> period, while its
Roman counterpart became increasingly decentralized and divided about the same time in what is known as the <color=#3366CC>Crisis</color>
<color=#3366CC>of the Third Century</color>. From the Eurasian steppe, horse-based nomads dominated a large part of the continent. The
development of the stirrup and the use of horse archers made the nomads a constant threat to sedentary civilizations.
In the 4th century CE, the Roman Empire split into western and eastern regions, with usually separate emperors. The

<color=#3366CC>Western Roman Empire</color> <color=#3366CC>fell</color> in 476 CE to German influence under <color=#3366CC>Odoacer</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Migration Period</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Germanic</color>
<color=#3366CC>peoples</color>. The Eastern Roman Empire, known as the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color>, was more long-lasting. In China, dynasties rose
and fell, but, in sharp contrast to the Mediterranean-European world, political unity was always eventually restored.
After the fall of the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Han dynasty</color> and the demise of the Three Kingdoms, nomadic tribes from the north began
to invade, causing many Chinese people to flee southward.
Post-classical
The post-classical period, dated roughly from 500 to 1500 CE, was characterized by the rise and spread of major
religions while civilization expanded to new parts of the world and trade between societies intensified. From the 10th to
13th centuries, the Medieval Warm Period in the Northern Hemisphere aided agriculture and led to population growth in
parts of Europe and Asia. It was followed by the <color=#3366CC>Little Ice Age</color>, which, along with the plagues of the 14th century, put
downward pressure on the population of Eurasia. Major inventions of the period were <color=#3366CC>gunpowder</color>, guns, and printing,
all of which originated in China.
The post-classical period encompasses the <color=#3366CC>early Muslim conquests</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Islamic Golden Age</color>, and the commencement
and expansion of the Arab slave trade, followed by the <color=#3366CC>Mongol invasions</color> and the founding of the Ottoman Empire.
South Asia had a series of <color=#3366CC>middle kingdoms</color>, followed by the establishment of Islamic empires in India.
In West Africa, the <color=#3366CC>Mali</color> and <color=#3366CC>Songhai Empires</color> rose. On the southeast coast of Africa, Arabic ports were established
where gold, <color=#3366CC>spices</color>, and other commodities were traded. This allowed Africa to join the Southeast Asia trading system,
bringing it into contact with Asia; this resulted in the Swahili culture.
China experienced the relatively successive Sui, Tang, <color=#3366CC>Song</color>, <color=#3366CC>Yuan</color>, and early <color=#3366CC>Ming dynasties</color>. Middle Eastern trade
routes along the Indian Ocean, and the Silk Road through the <color=#3366CC>Gobi Desert</color>, provided limited economic and cultural
contact between Asian and European civilizations. During the same period, civilizations in the Americas, such as the
<color=#3366CC>Mississippians</color>, <color=#3366CC>Aztecs</color>, Maya, and <color=#3366CC>Inca</color> reached their zenith.
West and Central Asia
Before the advent of Islam in the 7th century, the Middle East was dominated by the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sasanian</color> Empires,
which frequently fought each other for control of several disputed regions. The <color=#3366CC>birth of Islam</color> created a new contender
that quickly surpassed both of these empires. <color=#3366CC>Muhammad</color>, the founder of Islam, initiated the <color=#3366CC>early Muslim conquests</color> in
the 7th century. The subsequent <color=#3366CC>Abbasid Caliphate</color> oversaw the Islamic Golden Age, an era of learning, science, and
invention during which <color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, <color=#3366CC>art</color>, and <color=#3366CC>literature</color> flourished. Islamic civilization expanded both by conquest and
through its merchant economy. Merchants brought goods and their Islamic faith to China, India, Southeast Asia, and
Africa.
Arab domination of the Middle East ended in the mid-11th century with the arrival of the <color=#3366CC>Seljuk Turks</color>, migrating south
from the Turkic homelands. The Seljuks were challenged by Europe during the <color=#3366CC>Crusades</color>, a series of religious wars
aimed at rolling back Muslim territory and regaining control of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Land</color>. The Crusades were ultimately
unsuccessful and served more to weaken the Byzantine Empire. The Turks founded the Ottoman Empire in
modern-day Turkey around 1299. From the 10th century, the Abbasid Caliphate's African territory was consumed by
the <color=#3366CC>Fatimid Caliphate</color> centered on Egypt, who were supplanted by the <color=#3366CC>Ayyubids</color> in the 12th century, and then later by
the <color=#3366CC>Mamluks</color> in the 13th century. In the <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color> and <color=#3366CC>Western Sahara</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Almoravids</color> dominated from the 11th
century, until it was subsumed by the <color=#3366CC>Almohad Caliphate</color> in the 12th century. The Almohads' collapse gave rise to the
<color=#3366CC>Marinids</color> in Morocco, the Zayyanids in Algeria, and the Hafsids in Tunisia.
Steppe nomads from Central Asia, such as the Karluks and <color=#3366CC>Kipchaks</color>, continued to threaten sedentary societies in the
post-classical era, but they also faced incursions from the Arabs and Chinese. In the 8th century, Islam began to
penetrate the region and soon became the sole faith of most of the population. From the 9th to 13th centuries, Central
Asia was divided among several powerful states, including the <color=#3366CC>Samanid</color>, <color=#3366CC>Seljuk</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Khwarazmian Empires</color>. These
states were succeeded by the Mongols in the 13th century. In 1370, <color=#3366CC>Timur</color> conquered most of the region and founded
the <color=#3366CC>Timurid Empire</color>, which collapsed soon after his death. His descendants retained control of a core area in Central
Asia and Iran, overseeing the Timurid Renaissance of art and architecture.
Europe
Since at least the 4th century, Christianity has played a prominent role in shaping the culture, values, and institutions of
Western civilization, primarily through Catholicism and later also <color=#3366CC>Protestantism</color>. Europe during the <color=#3366CC>Early Middle Ages</color>
was characterized by depopulation, deurbanization, and barbarian invasions, all of which had begun in <color=#3366CC>late antiquity</color>.
The barbarian invaders formed their own new kingdoms in the remains of the Western Roman Empire. Christianity
expanded in Western Europe, and monasteries were founded. In the 7th and 8th centuries, the <color=#3366CC>Franks</color> under the
<color=#3366CC>Carolingian dynasty</color> established an empire covering much of Western Europe; it lasted until the 9th century, when it
succumbed to pressure from new invaders—the <color=#3366CC>Vikings</color>, Magyars, and Arabs. During the Carolingian era, churches
developed a form of musical notation called neume, which became the basis for the modern notation system. <color=#3366CC>Kievan</color>
<color=#3366CC>Rus'</color> expanded from its capital in <color=#3366CC>Kiev</color> to become the largest state in Europe by the 10th century. In 988, <color=#3366CC>Vladimir the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Great</color> adopted <color=#3366CC>Orthodox Christianity</color> as the state religion.
During the <color=#3366CC>High Middle Ages</color>, which began after 1000, the population of Europe increased as technological and
agricultural innovations allowed trade to flourish and crop yields to increase. The establishment of the <color=#3366CC>feudal system</color>
affected the structure of medieval society. It included manorialism, the organization of peasants into villages that owed
rents and labor service to nobles, and vassalage, a political structure whereby <color=#3366CC>knights</color> and lower-status nobles owed
military service to their overlords in return for the right to rents from lands and manors. Kingdoms became more
centralized after the decentralizing effects of the breakup of the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian Empire</color>. In 1054, the <color=#3366CC>Great Schism</color>
between the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Churches led to the prominent cultural differences between Western and
Eastern Europe. The <color=#3366CC>Crusades</color> were a series of religious wars waged by Christians to wrest control of the Holy Land
from the Muslims and succeeded for long enough to establish some <color=#3366CC>Crusader states</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>. Intellectual life was
marked by <color=#3366CC>scholasticism</color> and the founding of universities, while the building of Gothic cathedrals and churches was one
of the outstanding artistic achievements of the age.
The Caucasus was fought over in a <color=#3366CC>series of wars</color> between the Byzantine and Sasanian Empires. However, the two
opposing powers became exhausted due to continuous conflict. Hence, the Rashidun Caliphate was able to freely
expand into the region during the early Muslim conquests. The Seljuk Turks later subjugated <color=#3366CC>Armenia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Georgia</color> in
the 11th century. The Mongols subsequently invaded the Caucasus in the 13th century.
The <color=#3366CC>Mongols reached Europe</color> in 1236 and conquered Kievan Rus', along with briefly invading Poland and Hungary.
<color=#3366CC>Lithuania</color> cooperated with the Mongols but remained independent and, in the late 14th century, formed a personal
union with Poland. The <color=#3366CC>Late Middle Ages</color> were marked by difficulties and calamities. Famine, plague, and war
devastated the population of Western Europe. The <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color> alone killed approximately 75 to 200 million people
between 1347 and 1350. It was one of the deadliest pandemics in human history. Starting in Asia, the disease reached
the Mediterranean and Western Europe during the late 1340s, and killed tens of millions of Europeans in six years;
between a quarter and a third of the population perished.
Africa
Sub-Saharan Africa was home to many different civilizations. In <color=#3366CC>Nubia</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Kush</color> was succeeded by the
Christian kingdoms of <color=#3366CC>Makuria</color>, <color=#3366CC>Alodia</color>, and Nobatia. In the 7th century, Makuria conquered Nobatia to become the
dominant power in the region and resisted Muslim expansion. They later entered a severe decline following civil war
and Arab migrations to the Sudan and had disintegrated by the 15th century, giving rise to the <color=#3366CC>Funj Sultanate</color>. In the
<color=#3366CC>Horn of Africa</color>, Islam spread among the Somalis.
In the <color=#3366CC>Sahel</color> region of West Africa, the <color=#3366CC>Ghana Empire</color> formed between the 2nd and 8th centuries, while from the 7th
century the <color=#3366CC>Gao Empire</color> ruled to its east. Almoravid capture of royal Aoudaghost led to Ghana's conversion to Islam in
the 11th century, and climatic changes led to Ghana's conquest by its vassal Sosso in the 13th century. Sosso was
quickly overthrown by the <color=#3366CC>Mali Empire</color> who conquered Gao and dominated the <color=#3366CC>trans-Saharan trade</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Mossi</color>
<color=#3366CC>Kingdoms</color> were established to its south. To the east, the <color=#3366CC>Kanem–Bornu Empire</color> ruled from the 6th century, and it
projected power over the <color=#3366CC>Hausa Kingdoms</color>. The 15th century saw the crumbling of the Mali Empire, with the dominant
power in the region becoming the <color=#3366CC>Songhai Empire</color> centered on <color=#3366CC>Gao</color>.
In the forest regions of West Africa, various kingdoms and empires flourished, such as the <color=#3366CC>Yoruba</color> empires of Ife and

<color=#3366CC>Oyo</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Igbo</color> <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Nri</color>, the Edo <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Benin</color> (famous for its art), the Dagomba Kingdom of Dagbon, and
the Akan kingdoms of Bonoman and Adanse. They came into contact with the Portuguese in the 15th century, which
saw the start of the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic slave trade</color>.
In the western Congo Basin by the 13th century there were three main confederations of states: the Seven Kingdoms,
Mpemba, and one led by Vungu. In the 14th century, the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Kongo</color> emerged and dominated the region.
Further east, the <color=#3366CC>Luba Empire</color> was founded in the Upemba Depression in the 15th century. In the northern <color=#3366CC>Great</color>
<color=#3366CC>Lakes</color>, the Empire of Kitara rose around the 11th century, famed for its oral traditions. It collapsed in the 15th century
following Luo migrations to the region.
On the <color=#3366CC>Swahili coast</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Swahili city-states</color> thrived off of the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean trade</color> and gradually Islamized, giving rise to
the <color=#3366CC>Kilwa Sultanate</color> from the 10th century. Madagascar was settled by <color=#3366CC>Austronesian peoples</color> between the 5th and 7th
centuries, as societies organized at the behest of hasina. In Southern Africa, an early kingdom was Mapungubwe,
followed by the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe</color> in the 13th century, and the <color=#3366CC>Mutapa Empire</color> and Kingdom of Butua in the
15th century.
South Asia
After the fall of the Gupta Empire in 550 CE, <color=#3366CC>North India</color> was divided into a complex and fluid network of smaller
kingdoms. Early <color=#3366CC>Muslim incursions</color> began in the northwest in 711 CE, when the Arab Umayyad Caliphate <color=#3366CC>conquered</color>
much of present-day Pakistan. The Arab military advance was largely halted at that point, but Islam still spread in India,
largely due to the influence of Arab merchants along the western coast. The 9th century saw the <color=#3366CC>Tripartite Struggle</color> for
control of North India between the <color=#3366CC>Pratihara</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pala</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Rashtrakuta Empires</color>.
Post-classical dynasties in South India included those of the <color=#3366CC>Chalukyas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hoysalas</color>, and Cholas. Literature, architecture,
sculpture, and painting flourished under the patronage of these kings. Some of the other important states that emerged
in South India during this time included the <color=#3366CC>Bahmani Sultanate</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Vijayanagara Empire</color>.
Northeast Asia
After a period of relative disunity, <color=#3366CC>China</color> was reunified by the Sui dynasty in 589, later succeeded by the Tang dynasty
in 618. Both dynasties instituted the long-lasting <color=#3366CC>imperial examination</color> system. China later competed with <color=#3366CC>Tibet</color>
(618–842) for control of areas in Inner Asia. However, the Tang dynasty eventually splintered. After <color=#3366CC>half a century of</color>
<color=#3366CC>turmoil</color>, the Song dynasty reunified much of China. Pressure from nomadic empires to the north became increasingly
urgent. By 1127, northern China had been lost to the Jurchens in the <color=#3366CC>Jin–Song Wars</color>, and the Mongols <color=#3366CC>conquered all of</color>
<color=#3366CC>China</color> in 1279. After about a century of Mongol Yuan dynasty rule, the ethnic Chinese reasserted control with the
founding of the Ming dynasty in 1368.
In <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>, the imperial lineage was established during the 3rd century CE, and a centralized state developed during the
<color=#3366CC>Yamato period</color> (c. 300–710). Buddhism was introduced, and there was an emphasis on the adoption of elements of
Chinese culture and Confucianism. The Nara period (710–794) was characterized by the appearance of a nascent
<color=#3366CC>literary culture</color>, as well as the development of Buddhist-inspired artwork and architecture. The <color=#3366CC>Heian period</color> (794–1185)
saw the peak of imperial power, followed by the rise of militarized clans and the <color=#3366CC>samurai</color>. It was during the Heian period
that <color=#3366CC>Murasaki Shikibu</color> penned <color=#3366CC>The Tale of Genji</color>, sometimes considered the world's first novel. From 1185 to 1868,
Japan was dominated by powerful regional lords (daimyos) and the military rule of warlords (<color=#3366CC>shoguns</color>) such as the
Ashikaga and <color=#3366CC>Tokugawa shogunates</color>. The emperor remained but did not wield significant influence. Meanwhile, the
power of merchants grew. An influential art style known as <color=#3366CC>ukiyo-e</color> arose during the Tokugawa years, consisting of
woodblock prints which originally depicted famous courtesans.

Post-classical <color=#3366CC>Korea</color> saw the end of the <color=#3366CC>Three Kingdoms</color> era, in which the kingdoms of <color=#3366CC>Goguryeo</color>, <color=#3366CC>Baekje</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Silla</color>
had competed for hegemony. This period ended when Silla conquered Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668, marking
the beginning of the Northern and Southern States period, with <color=#3366CC>Unified Silla</color> in the south and <color=#3366CC>Balhae</color>, a successor state
to Goguryeo, in the north. In 892 CE, this arrangement reverted to the <color=#3366CC>Later Three Kingdoms</color>, with Goguryeo emerging
as dominant, unifying the entire peninsula by 936. The founding Goryeo dynasty ruled until 1392, succeeded by the
<color=#3366CC>Joseon dynasty</color>, which ruled for approximately 500 years.
In <color=#3366CC>Mongolia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Genghis Khan</color> united various Mongol and Turkic tribes under one banner in 1206. The <color=#3366CC>Mongol Empire</color>
expanded from North Asia to comprise all of China and Central Asia, as well as large parts of Russia and the Middle
East, to become the largest contiguous empire in history. After <color=#3366CC>Möngke Khan</color> died in 1259, the Mongol Empire was

<color=#3366CC>divided into four successor states</color>: the <color=#3366CC>Yuan Dynasty</color> in China, the <color=#3366CC>Chagatai Khanate</color> in Central Asia, the <color=#3366CC>Golden Horde</color>
in Eastern Europe and Russia, and the <color=#3366CC>Ilkhanate</color> in Iran.
Southeast Asia
The Southeast Asian polity of <color=#3366CC>Funan</color>, which had originated in the 2nd century CE, went into decline in the 6th century
as Chinese trade routes shifted away from its ports. It was replaced by the <color=#3366CC>Khmer Empire</color> in 802 CE. The capital city of
the Khmers at <color=#3366CC>Angkor</color> was the most extensive city in the world before the industrial age and contained <color=#3366CC>Angkor Wat</color>, the
world's largest religious monument. The <color=#3366CC>Sukhothai</color> (mid-13th century) and <color=#3366CC>Ayutthaya Kingdoms</color> (1351) were major
powers of the <color=#3366CC>Thais</color>, who were influenced by the Khmers.
Starting in the 9th century, the <color=#3366CC>Pagan Kingdom</color> rose to prominence in modern <color=#3366CC>Myanmar</color>. Its collapse brought about
political fragmentation that ended with the rise of the Toungoo Empire in the 16th century. Other notable kingdoms of
the period include <color=#3366CC>Srivijaya</color> and Lavo (both coming into prominence in the 7th century), <color=#3366CC>Champa</color> and Hariphunchai

(both about 750), <color=#3366CC>Đai Viet</color> (968), <color=#3366CC>Lan Na</color> (13th century), <color=#3366CC>Majapahit</color> (1293), <color=#3366CC>Lan Xang</color> (1353), and Ava (1365). Hinduism
and Buddhism had been spreading in Southeast Asia since the 1st century CE when, beginning in the 13th century,
Islam arrived and made its way to regions such as present-day Indonesia. This period also saw the emergence of the
Malay states, including <color=#3366CC>Brunei</color> and <color=#3366CC>Malacca</color>. In the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color>, several polities were formed such as Tondo, Cebu, and
<color=#3366CC>Butuan</color>.
Oceania
The <color=#3366CC>Polynesians</color>, descendants of the <color=#3366CC>Lapita peoples</color>, colonized vast reaches of Remote Oceania beginning around
1000 CE. Their voyages resulted in the colonization of hundreds of islands including the <color=#3366CC>Marquesas</color>, Hawaii, <color=#3366CC>Rapa Nui</color>
(Easter Island), and New Zealand.
The <color=#3366CC>Tui Tonga Empire</color> was founded in the 10th century CE and expanded between 1250 and 1500. Tongan culture,
language, and hegemony spread widely throughout eastern <color=#3366CC>Melanesia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Micronesia</color>, and central <color=#3366CC>Polynesia</color> during this
period. They influenced east 'Uvea, <color=#3366CC>Rotuma</color>, Futuna, <color=#3366CC>Samoa</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Niue</color>, as well as specific islands and parts of
Micronesia, <color=#3366CC>Vanuatu</color>, and <color=#3366CC>New Caledonia</color>. In Northern Australia, there is evidence that <color=#3366CC>Aboriginal Australians</color> regularly
<color=#3366CC>traded with Makassan trepangers</color> from Indonesia before the arrival of Europeans. In Aboriginal societies, leadership
was based on achievement while the social structure of Polynesian societies was characterized by hereditary
<color=#3366CC>chiefdoms</color>.
Americas
In North America, this period saw the rise of the <color=#3366CC>Mississippian culture</color> in the modern-day United States c. 950 CE,
marked by the extensive 11th-century urban complex at <color=#3366CC>Cahokia</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Ancestral Puebloans</color> and their predecessors
(9th–13th centuries) built extensive permanent settlements, including stone structures that remained the largest
buildings in North America until the 19th century.
In Mesoamerica, the <color=#3366CC>Teotihuacan civilization</color> fell, and the <color=#3366CC>classic Maya collapse</color> occurred. The <color=#3366CC>Aztec Empire</color> came to
dominate much of Mesoamerica in the 14th and 15th centuries.
In South America, the 15th century saw the rise of the Inca. The <color=#3366CC>Inca Empire</color>, with its capital at <color=#3366CC>Cusco</color>, spanned the
entire <color=#3366CC>Andes</color>, making it the most extensive <color=#3366CC>pre-Columbian civilization</color>. The Inca were prosperous and advanced, known
for an excellent <color=#3366CC>road system</color> and elegant stonework.
Early modern
The early modern period is the era following the European Middle Ages until 1789 or 1800. A common break with the
medieval period is placed between 1450 and 1500, which includes a number of significant events: the fall of
<color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> to the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color>, the spread of <color=#3366CC>printing</color>, and European voyages of discovery to America and
along the African coast. The nature of warfare evolved as the size and organization of military forces on land and sea
increased, alongside the wider propagation of gunpowder. The early modern period is significant for the start of
proto-globalization, increasingly centralized bureaucratic states and early forms of <color=#3366CC>capitalism</color>. European powers also
began colonizing large parts of the world through maritime empires: first the <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color> and <color=#3366CC>Spanish Empires</color>, then the

<color=#3366CC>French</color>, <color=#3366CC>English</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Dutch Empires</color>. Historians still debate the causes of Europe's rise, which is known as the <color=#3366CC>Great</color>
<color=#3366CC>Divergence</color>.
Capitalist economies emerged, initially in the <color=#3366CC>northern Italian republics</color> and some Asian port cities. European states
practiced <color=#3366CC>mercantilism</color> by implementing one-sided trade policies designed to benefit the mother country at the expense
of its colonies. Starting at the end of the 15th century, the Portuguese established trading posts across Africa, Asia, and
Brazil, for commodities like gold and spices while also practicing <color=#3366CC>slavery</color>. In the 17th century, private chartered
companies were established, such as the <color=#3366CC>English East India Company</color> in 1600 – often described as the first
<color=#3366CC>multinational corporation</color> – and the <color=#3366CC>Dutch East India Company</color> in 1602. Meanwhile, in much of the European sphere,
<color=#3366CC>serfdom</color> declined and eventually disappeared while the power of the Catholic Church waned.
The <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color> was the first period in which the <color=#3366CC>Old World</color> engaged in substantial cultural, material, and
biological exchange with the <color=#3366CC>New World</color>. It began in the late 15th century, when Portugal and Castile sent the first
exploratory voyages to the Americas, where <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color> first arrived in 1492. Global integration continued as
<color=#3366CC>European colonization of the Americas</color> initiated the <color=#3366CC>Columbian exchange</color>: the exchange of plants, animals, foods,
human populations (including slaves), <color=#3366CC>communicable diseases</color>, and culture between the <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color> and <color=#3366CC>Western</color>
<color=#3366CC>Hemispheres</color>. It was one of history's most important global events, involving ecology and agriculture. New crops
brought from the Americas by 16th-century European seafarers substantially contributed to world population growth.
West and Central Asia
The Ottoman Empire quickly came to dominate the Middle East after conquering Constantinople in 1453, which marked
the end of the Byzantine Empire. Persia came under the rule of the <color=#3366CC>Safavids</color> in 1501, succeeded by the Afshars in
1736, the Zands in 1751, and the <color=#3366CC>Qajars</color> in 1794. The Safavids <color=#3366CC>established</color> <color=#3366CC>Shia Islam</color> as Persia's official religion, thus
giving Persia a separate identity from its <color=#3366CC>Sunni</color> neighbors. Along with the <color=#3366CC>Mughals</color> in India, the Ottomans and Safavids
are known as the gunpowder empires because of their early adoption of firearms. Throughout the 16th century, the
Ottomans conquered all of North Africa save for Morocco, which came under the rule of the <color=#3366CC>Saadi dynasty</color> at the same
time, and then the Alawi dynasty in the 17th century.
The Uzbeks replaced the <color=#3366CC>Timurids</color> as the preeminent power in Central Asia by the 16th century. In the early 18th
century, Russia began <color=#3366CC>its expansion into Central Asia</color> that lasted until the late 19th century.
Europe
The early modern period in Europe was an era of intense intellectual ferment. The <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> – the "rebirth" of
classical culture, beginning <color=#3366CC>in Italy</color> in the 14th century and extending into the 16th – comprised the rediscovery of the
<color=#3366CC>classical world</color>'s cultural, scientific, and technological achievements, and the economic and social rise of Europe. This
period is also celebrated for its artistic and literary attainments. <color=#3366CC>Petrarch</color>'s poetry, <color=#3366CC>Giovanni Boccaccio</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Decameron</color>,
and the paintings and sculptures of <color=#3366CC>Leonardo da Vinci</color> and <color=#3366CC>Albrecht Dürer</color>, as part of the Northern Renaissance, are
some of the great works of the age. After the Renaissance came the <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color>, an anti-clerical theological and social
movement started in Germany by <color=#3366CC>Martin Luther</color> that resulted in the creation of <color=#3366CC>Protestant Christianity</color>.
The Renaissance also engendered a culture of inquisitiveness which ultimately led to <color=#3366CC>humanism</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Scientific</color>
<color=#3366CC>Revolution</color>, an effort to understand the natural world through direct observation and experiment. The success of the
new scientific techniques inspired attempts to apply them to political and social affairs, known as the <color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color>, by
thinkers such as <color=#3366CC>John Locke</color> and <color=#3366CC>Immanuel Kant</color>. This development was accompanied by <color=#3366CC>secularization</color> as a continued
decline of the influence of religious beliefs and authorities in the public and private spheres. <color=#3366CC>Johannes Gutenberg</color>'s
invention of <color=#3366CC>movable type</color> printing in 1440 helped spread the ideas of the new intellectual movements.
In addition to changes wrought by incipient capitalism and colonialism, early modern Europeans experienced an

increase in the power of the state. Absolute monarchs in <color=#3366CC>France</color>, <color=#3366CC>Russia</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Habsburg lands</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Prussia</color> produced
powerful centralized states, with strong armies and efficient bureaucracies, all under the control of the king. In Russia,
<color=#3366CC>Ivan the Terrible</color> was crowned in 1547 as the first <color=#3366CC>tsar</color> of Russia, and by annexing the Turkic khanates in the east,
transformed Russia into a regional power, eventually <color=#3366CC>replacing</color> the <color=#3366CC>Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</color> as a major power
in Eastern Europe. At the end of the 18th century, the <color=#3366CC>Russian Empire</color> began its conquest of the Caucasus. The
countries of Western Europe, while expanding prodigiously through technological advances and colonial conquest,
competed with each other economically and militarily in a state of almost constant war. Wars of particular note included

the <color=#3366CC>Thirty Years' War</color>, the <color=#3366CC>War of the Spanish Succession</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Seven Years' War</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>French Revolutionary Wars</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color>, starting in 1789, laid the groundwork for liberal democracy by overthrowing monarchy. It led to
the rise of <color=#3366CC>Napoleon Bonaparte</color> and the subsequent <color=#3366CC>Napoleonic Wars</color> of the early 19th century.
Africa

In the <color=#3366CC>Horn of Africa</color>, there was the <color=#3366CC>Oromo expansion</color> in the 16th century, which weakened <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia</color> and caused <color=#3366CC>Adal</color>'s
collapse. <color=#3366CC>Ajuran</color> was succeeded by the Geledi Sultanate. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Ethiopia rapidly
expanded.
In West Africa, the <color=#3366CC>Songhai Empire</color> fell to Moroccan invasion in the late 16th century. They were succeeded by the
Bamana Empire. The <color=#3366CC>Fula jihads</color> beginning in the 18th century led to the establishment of the <color=#3366CC>Sokoto Caliphate</color>, the
Massina Empire, and the <color=#3366CC>Tukulor Empire</color>. In the forest regions, the <color=#3366CC>Asante Empire</color> was established in present-day
Ghana. Between 1515 and 1800, 8 million Africans were exported in the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic slave trade</color>.
In the western Congo Basin, <color=#3366CC>Kongo</color> fought three wars against the Portuguese who had begun colonizing Angola,
ending in the conquest of Ndongo in the 17th century. Further east, the <color=#3366CC>Lunda Empire</color> rose to dominate the region. It
fell to the Chokwe in the 19th century. In the northern <color=#3366CC>Great Lakes</color>, the kingdoms of Bunyoro-Kitara, Buganda, and
Rwanda struggled for hegemony among others.
<color=#3366CC>Kilwa</color> was conquered by the Portuguese in the 16th century as they began colonizing Mozambique. They were
defeated by the <color=#3366CC>Omani Empire</color> who took control of the <color=#3366CC>Swahili coast</color>. In Madagascar, the 16th century onward saw the
emergence of <color=#3366CC>Imerina</color>, the Betsileo kingdoms, and the Sakalava empire; Imerina conquered most of the island in the
19th century. In the Zambezi Basin, <color=#3366CC>Mutapa</color> was followed by the Rozvi Empire, with <color=#3366CC>Maravi</color> around <color=#3366CC>Lake Malawi</color> to its
north. Mthwakazi succeeded Rozvi. Further south, the Dutch began <color=#3366CC>colonizing South Africa</color> in the 16th century, but lost
it to the British. In the 19th century, Dutch settlers formed various <color=#3366CC>Boer Republics</color> while the <color=#3366CC>Mfecane</color> ravaged the region
and led to the establishment of various African kingdoms.
South Asia
In the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color> was established under <color=#3366CC>Babur</color> in 1526 and lasted for two centuries.
Starting in the northwest, it brought the entire subcontinent under Muslim rule by the late 17th century, except for the
southernmost Indian provinces, which remained independent. To resist the Muslim rulers, the Hindu <color=#3366CC>Maratha Empire</color>
was founded by <color=#3366CC>Shivaji</color> on the western coast in 1674. The Marathas gradually gained territory from the Mughals over
several decades, particularly in the <color=#3366CC>Mughal–Maratha Wars</color> (1680–1707).
<color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color> developed at the end of the 15th century from the spiritual teachings of ten <color=#3366CC>gurus</color>. In 1799, <color=#3366CC>Ranjit Singh</color>
established the <color=#3366CC>Sikh Empire</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Punjab</color>.
Northeast Asia
In 1644, the Ming <color=#3366CC>were supplanted</color> by the <color=#3366CC>Manchu</color> <color=#3366CC>Qing</color>, the last conquest dynasty, which ruled China until 1912. By
the late 18th century, Russia completed <color=#3366CC>its subjugation of Siberia</color>, with the territory between the Ural Mountains and the
Pacific Ocean falling under its control.
Japan experienced its Azuchi–Momoyama period (1568–1600), followed by the <color=#3366CC>Edo period</color> (1600–1868). The Korean
Joseon dynasty (1392–1910) ruled throughout this period, repelling invasions from Japan and China in the 16th and
17th centuries. Expanded maritime trade with Europe significantly affected China and Japan during this period,
particularly through the Portuguese in <color=#3366CC>Macau</color> and the Dutch in Nagasaki. However, China and Japan later pursued
<color=#3366CC>isolationist</color> policies designed to eliminate foreign influences.
Southeast Asia
In 1511, the Portuguese overthrew the <color=#3366CC>Malacca Sultanate</color> in present-day Malaysia and Indonesian <color=#3366CC>Sumatra</color>. The
Portuguese held this important trading territory (and the valuable associated navigational strait) until overthrown by the
Dutch in 1641. The <color=#3366CC>Johor Sultanate</color>, centered on the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, became the dominant trading
power in the region. European colonization expanded with the Dutch in <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>, the Portuguese in Timor, and the
Spaniards in the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color>.
Oceania
The Pacific Islands of Oceania were also affected by European contact, starting with the <color=#3366CC>circumnavigational voyage</color> of
<color=#3366CC>Ferdinand Magellan</color> (1519–1522), who landed in the <color=#3366CC>Marianas</color> and other islands. <color=#3366CC>Abel Tasman</color> (1642–1644) sailed to
present-day <color=#3366CC>Australia</color>, <color=#3366CC>New Zealand</color>, and nearby islands. <color=#3366CC>James Cook</color> (1768–1779) made the first recorded European
contact with <color=#3366CC>Hawaii</color>. In 1788, Britain founded its first Australian colony.
Americas
Several European powers colonized the Americas, largely displacing the native populations and conquering the
advanced civilizations of the Aztecs and Inca. Diseases introduced by Europeans devastated American societies, killing
60–90 million people by 1600 and reducing the population by 90–95%. In some cases, colonial policies included the
deliberate <color=#3366CC>genocide of indigenous peoples</color>. Spain, Portugal, Britain, and France all made extensive territorial claims,
and they undertook <color=#3366CC>large-scale settlement</color>, including the importation of large numbers of African slaves. One side-effect
of the slave trade was cultural exchange through which various African traditions found their way to the Americas,
including cuisine, music, and dance. Portugal claimed <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color>, while Spain seized the rest of South America,
Mesoamerica, and southern North America. The Spaniards mined and exported prodigious amounts of gold and silver,
leading to a surge in inflation known as the <color=#3366CC>Price Revolution</color> in the 16th and 17th centuries in Western Europe.
In North America, Britain colonized the east coast while France settled the central region. Russia made incursions into
the northwest coast of North America. France lost its North American territory to England and Spain after the Seven
Years' War (1756–1763). Britain's <color=#3366CC>Thirteen Colonies</color> <color=#3366CC>declared independence as the United States</color> in 1776, ratified by
the <color=#3366CC>Treaty of Paris</color> in 1783, ending the <color=#3366CC>American Revolutionary War</color>. In 1791, African slaves <color=#3366CC>launched a successful</color>
<color=#3366CC>rebellion</color> in the French colony of Saint-Domingue. France won back its continental claims from Spain in 1800, but sold
them to the United States in the <color=#3366CC>Louisiana Purchase</color> of 1803.
Modern
Long nineteenth century
The long nineteenth century traditionally starts with the <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color> in 1789, and lasts until the outbreak of World
War I in 1914. It saw the global spread of the Industrial Revolution, the greatest transformation of the world economy
since the Neolithic Revolution. The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain around 1770 and used new modes of
production—the factory, <color=#3366CC>mass production</color>, and <color=#3366CC>mechanization</color>—to manufacture a wide array of goods faster while using
less labor than previously required. As a consequence of the tensions between the ruling elite and the working class
that had been raised by the Industrial Revolution, this led to massive political upheavals, with individuals such as <color=#3366CC>Karl</color>
<color=#3366CC>Marx</color> being major figureheads within the movement.
Industrialization raised the global standard of living but caused upheaval as factory owners and workers clashed over
wages and working conditions. Along with industrialization came modern <color=#3366CC>globalization</color>, the increasing interconnection
of world regions in the economic, political, and cultural spheres. Globalization began in the early 19th century and was
enabled by improved transportation technologies such as railroads and <color=#3366CC>steamships</color>.
European empires <color=#3366CC>lost territories in Latin America</color>, which <color=#3366CC>won independence</color> by the 1820s through military campaigns,
but expanded elsewhere as their industrial economies gave them an advantage over the rest of the world. Britain
gained control of the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color>, <color=#3366CC>Burma</color>, Malaya, North Borneo, <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color>, and Aden; the French took
<color=#3366CC>Indochina</color>; and the Dutch cemented their rule over <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>. The British also colonized Canada, Australia, New
Zealand, and South Africa, with large numbers of British colonists emigrating to these colonies, displacing indigenous
peoples in several areas.
Russia colonized large pre-agricultural areas of Siberia. The United States completed its <color=#3366CC>westward expansion</color>,
establishing control over the territory from the Atlantic to the Pacific coast.
In the late 19th century to the early 20th century, the European powers, driven by the <color=#3366CC>Second Industrial Revolution</color>,
rapidly <color=#3366CC>conquered and colonized almost the entirety of Africa</color>. Only Ethiopia and <color=#3366CC>Liberia</color> remained independent.
Imperial rule in Africa involved many atrocities such as <color=#3366CC>those in the Congo Free State</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Herero and Nama</color>
<color=#3366CC>genocide</color>.
Within Europe, economic and military competition fostered the creation and consolidation of nation-states, and other
ethno-cultural communities began to identify themselves as distinctive nations with aspirations for their own cultural and
political autonomy. This <color=#3366CC>nationalism</color> became important to peoples across the world in the 19th and 20th centuries. In
the first wave of democratization, between 1828 and 1926, democratic institutions were established in 33 countries
worldwide.
Most of the world <color=#3366CC>abolished slavery</color> and serfdom in the 19th century. Over several decades, beginning in the late 19th
century and continuing throughout the 20th, in many countries the <color=#3366CC>women's suffrage</color> movement won women the right to
vote, and women began to enjoy greater access to education and to professions beyond domestic employment.
In response to encroachment by European powers, several countries undertook programs of industrialization and
political reform along Western lines. The <color=#3366CC>Meiji Restoration</color> in <color=#3366CC>Japan</color> led to the establishment of a colonial empire, while
the <color=#3366CC>Tanzimat</color> reforms in the Ottoman Empire did little to slow the Ottoman decline. China achieved some success with
its <color=#3366CC>Self-Strengthening Movement</color> but was devastated by the <color=#3366CC>Taiping Rebellion</color>, history's bloodiest civil war, which
between 1850 and 1864 killed 20–30 million people.
By the end of the century, the United States became the world's largest economy. During the <color=#3366CC>Second Industrial</color>

<color=#3366CC>Revolution</color>, new technological advances, involving <color=#3366CC>electric power</color>, the <color=#3366CC>internal combustion engine</color>, and <color=#3366CC>assembly-line</color>
manufacturing, further increased productivity. Technological innovations also provided new avenues for artistic
expression through the media of <color=#3366CC>photography</color>, <color=#3366CC>sound recording</color>, and <color=#3366CC>film</color>.
Meanwhile, <color=#3366CC>industrial pollution</color> and <color=#3366CC>environmental degradation</color> accelerated drastically. <color=#3366CC>Balloon flight</color> had been invented
in the late 18th century, but it was only at the beginning of the 20th century that <color=#3366CC>powered aircraft were developed</color>.
The 20th century opened with Europe at an apex of wealth and power. Much of the world was under its direct colonial
control or its indirect influence through heavily Europeanized nations like the United States and Japan. As the century
unfolded, however, the global system dominated by rival powers experienced severe strains and ultimately yielded to a
more fluid structure of independent <color=#3366CC>nation states</color>.
World wars
This transformation was catalyzed by wars of unparalleled scope and devastation. <color=#3366CC>World War I</color> was a global conflict
from 1914 to 1918 between the <color=#3366CC>Allies</color>, led by France, Russia, and the United Kingdom, and the <color=#3366CC>Central Powers</color>, led by
<color=#3366CC>Germany</color>, <color=#3366CC>Austria-Hungary</color>, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria. It had an estimated death toll ranging from 10 to 22.5
million and resulted in the collapse of four empires – the Austro-Hungarian, German, Ottoman, and Russian Empires.
Its new emphasis on industrial technology had made traditional military tactics obsolete.
The <color=#3366CC>Armenian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Assyrian</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Greek genocides</color> saw the systematic destruction, mass murder, and expulsion of those
populations in the Ottoman Empire. From 1918 to 1920, the <color=#3366CC>Spanish flu</color> caused the deaths of at least 25 million people.
In the war's aftermath, a <color=#3366CC>League of Nations</color> was formed in the hope of averting future international conflicts, and
powerful ideologies rose to prominence. The <color=#3366CC>Russian Revolution</color> of 1917 created the Soviet Union, which would be
known as the first communist state, while the 1920s and 1930s saw <color=#3366CC>fascist</color> political parties gain control in Italy and
<color=#3366CC>Germany</color>. The Soviet Union, during <color=#3366CC>Stalinist</color> rule from 1924 to 1953, committed countless atrocities against its own
people, including mass purges, <color=#3366CC>forced labor camps</color>, and <color=#3366CC>widespread famine</color> caused by state policies.
Ongoing national rivalries, exacerbated by the economic turmoil of the <color=#3366CC>Great Depression</color>, helped precipitate <color=#3366CC>World War</color>
<color=#3366CC>II</color>. In that war, the vast majority of the world's countries, including all the <color=#3366CC>great powers</color>, fought as part of two opposing

<color=#3366CC>military alliances</color>: the <color=#3366CC>Allies</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Axis</color>. The leading Axis powers were <color=#3366CC>Nazi Germany</color>, <color=#3366CC>Imperial Japan</color>, and the
Kingdom of Italy; while the United Kingdom, the United States, the Soviet Union, and the <color=#3366CC>Republic of China</color> were the
"Big Four" Allied powers.
The <color=#3366CC>militaristic</color> governments of Germany and Japan pursued <color=#3366CC>imperialist</color> <color=#3366CC>expansionism</color>. In the course of doing so,
Germany killed <color=#3366CC>6 million Jews</color> and millions of non-Jews under the rule of <color=#3366CC>Adolf Hitler</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Nazi Party</color>, while Japan
<color=#3366CC>murdered</color> millions of Chinese. The war also saw the introduction and use of <color=#3366CC>nuclear weapons</color>, which brought
unprecedented destruction and ultimately led to Japan's surrender. Estimates of the war's total casualties range from
55 to 80 million.
Contemporary history
When World War II ended in 1945, the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color> was founded in the hope of preventing future wars, as the
<color=#3366CC>League of Nations</color> had been formed following World War I. The United Nations championed the human rights
movement, in 1948 adopting the <color=#3366CC>Universal Declaration of Human Rights</color>. Several European countries formed what
would later become the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>.
World War II had opened the way for the advance of communism into Eastern and Central Europe, China, <color=#3366CC>North Korea</color>,
<color=#3366CC>North Vietnam</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Cuba</color>. To <color=#3366CC>contain</color> this advance, the United States established a global network of alliances. The
largest, <color=#3366CC>NATO</color>, was established in 1949. In response, in 1955 the Soviet Union and its Eastern European allies formed
the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color>.
The United States and the Soviet Union emerged as the primary global powers in the aftermath of World War II. Both
nations harbored deep suspicions and fears about the global spread of the other's political-economic
system—capitalism for the United States and communism for the Soviet Union. This mutual distrust sparked the <color=#3366CC>Cold</color>
<color=#3366CC>War</color>, a 45-year stand-off and <color=#3366CC>arms race</color> between the two nations and their allies.
With the development of nuclear weapons during World War II and their subsequent <color=#3366CC>proliferation</color>, all of humanity was
put at risk of <color=#3366CC>nuclear war</color> between the two superpowers, as demonstrated by many incidents, most prominently the
October 1962 <color=#3366CC>Cuban Missile Crisis</color>. Such war being viewed as impractical, the superpowers instead waged <color=#3366CC>proxy wars</color>
in non-nuclear-armed <color=#3366CC>Third World</color> countries. The Cold War ended peacefully in 1991 after the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union collapsed</color>,
partly due to its inability to compete economically with the United States and Western Europe.
Cold War preparations to deter or fight a third world war accelerated advances in technologies that, though
conceptualized before World War II, had been implemented for that war's exigencies, such as <color=#3366CC>jet aircraft</color>, <color=#3366CC>rocketry</color>, and
computers. In the decades after World War II, these advances led to jet travel; <color=#3366CC>artificial satellites</color> with innumerable
applications, including <color=#3366CC>GPS</color>; and the <color=#3366CC>Internet</color>, which in the 1990s began to gain traction as a form of communication.
These inventions revolutionized the movement of people, ideas, and information.
The second half of the 20th century also saw groundbreaking scientific and technological developments such as the
worldwide eradication of smallpox, the <color=#3366CC>Green Revolution</color> in agriculture, the discovery of <color=#3366CC>plate tectonics</color>, the <color=#3366CC>moon</color>
<color=#3366CC>landings</color>, crewed and uncrewed <color=#3366CC>exploration of space</color>, advances in <color=#3366CC>energy technologies</color>, and foundational discoveries in
<color=#3366CC>physics</color>. These technical innovations had far-reaching effects. During the 20th century, the world's population
quadrupled to six billion, while world economic output increased by a factor of 20. Toward the end of the 20th century,
the rate of <color=#3366CC>population growth</color> started to decline.
<color=#3366CC>Public health</color> measures and advances in <color=#3366CC>medical science</color> contributed to a sharp increase in global <color=#3366CC>life expectancy</color> at
birth from about 31 years in 1900 to over 66 years in 2000. In 1820, 75% of humanity lived on less than one dollar a
day, while in 2001 only about 20% did. At the same time, economic inequality increased both within individual countries
and between rich and poor countries. The importance of public education had already begun to increase in the 18th
and 19th centuries, but it was not until the end of the 20th and the beginning of the 21st century that compulsory free
education was provided to most children worldwide.
In China, the <color=#3366CC>Maoist</color> government implemented industrialization and <color=#3366CC>collectivization</color> policies as part of the <color=#3366CC>Great Leap</color>
<color=#3366CC>Forward</color>, leading to the <color=#3366CC>starvation deaths</color> of 30–40 million people. China later entered a period of <color=#3366CC>economic</color>
<color=#3366CC>liberalization</color> and rapid growth.

In the postwar decades, in a process of <color=#3366CC>decolonization</color>, the <color=#3366CC>African</color>, <color=#3366CC>Asian</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Oceanian</color> colonies of European empires
won their formal independence. Postcolonial states in Africa struggled to grow their economies. The <color=#3366CC>Near East</color>

experienced numerous conflicts, including the <color=#3366CC>Iran–Iraq War</color>, the <color=#3366CC>first</color> and <color=#3366CC>second Gulf wars</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Syrian civil war</color>,
as well as <color=#3366CC>tensions and conflicts between Israel and Palestine</color>.
The early 21st century was marked by growing <color=#3366CC>economic globalization</color>, as well as the <color=#3366CC>Great Recession</color>.
Communications expanded, with <color=#3366CC>smartphones</color> and <color=#3366CC>social media</color> becoming ubiquitous worldwide by the mid-2010s. By
the early 2020s, <color=#3366CC>artificial intelligence</color> systems improved to the point of outperforming humans at many circumscribed
tasks, initiating the <color=#3366CC>AI boom</color> in the early 2020s.
The influence of religion continued to decline in many Western countries, while some parts of the Muslim world saw the
rise of <color=#3366CC>fundamentalist movements</color>. In 2020, the <color=#3366CC>COVID-19 pandemic</color> substantially disrupted global trade, caused
recessions in the global economy, and spurred cultural paradigm shifts. <color=#3366CC>Environmental degradation</color>, including
multifarious forms of <color=#3366CC>pollution</color>, and <color=#3366CC>global warming</color> became increasingly evident, while <color=#3366CC>mitigation efforts</color> made gradual
progress.
Academic research
The study of human history has a long tradition, and early precursors were already practiced in the ancient period as
attempts to provide comprehensive accounts of the history of the world. Most research before the 20th century focused
on histories of individual communities and societies after the prehistoric period. This changed in the late 20th century,
when attempts to integrate the diverse narratives into a common context reaching back to the emergence of the first
humans became a central research topic. This transition to a widened perspective was accompanied by questioning
<color=#3366CC>Eurocentrism</color> and the Western-focused perspective that had previously dominated academic history.
Like in other historical disciplines, the <color=#3366CC>methodology</color> of analyzing textual sources to construct narratives and
interpretations of past events plays a central role in the study of human history. The scope of its topic poses the unique
challenge of synthesizing a coherent and comprehensive narrative spanning different cultures, regions, and time
periods while taking diverse individual perspectives into account. This is also reflected in its <color=#3366CC>interdisciplinary approach</color>
by integrating insights from fields belonging to the <color=#3366CC>humanities</color> and the <color=#3366CC>social</color>, biological, and physical sciences, such as

other <color=#3366CC>historical disciplines</color>, <color=#3366CC>archaeology</color>, <color=#3366CC>anthropology</color>, <color=#3366CC>linguistics</color>, <color=#3366CC>genetics</color>, <color=#3366CC>paleontology</color>, and <color=#3366CC>geology</color>. The
interdisciplinary approach is of particular importance to the study of human history before the invention of writing.
Periodization
To provide an accessible overview, historians divide human history into different periods organized around key themes,
events, or developments that have shaped human societies over time. The number of periods and their time frames
depend on the chosen topics, and the transitions between periods are often more fluid than static periodization
schemes suggest.
A traditionally influential periodization in European scholarship distinguishes between the ancient, medieval, and
modern periods, organized around historical events responsible for major shifts in political, economic, and cultural
structures to mark the transitions between the periods: first the fall of the Western Roman Empire and later the
emergence of the Renaissance. Another periodization divides human history into three periods based on the way
humans engage with nature to produce goods. The first transition happened with the emergence of agriculture and
husbandry to replace hunting and gathering as the main means of food production. The Industrial Revolution
constitutes the second transition.
A further approach uses the relations between societies to divide the history of the world into the periods of Middle
Eastern dominance before 500 BCE, Eurasian cultural balance until 1500 CE, and Western dominance afterwards. The
invention of writing is often used to demarcate prehistory from the ancient period, while another approach divides early
history based on the type of tools used in the Stone, Bronze, and Iron Ages. Historians focusing on religion and culture
identify the Axial Age as a key turning point that laid the spiritual and philosophical foundations of many of the world's
major civilizations. Some historians draw on elements from different approaches to arrive at a more nuanced
periodization.
Sargasso Sea
The Sargasso Sea is a region of the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic Ocean</color> bounded by four <color=#3366CC>currents</color> forming an ocean gyre. It is the only
named <color=#3366CC>sea</color> without land boundaries. It is distinguished from other parts of the Atlantic Ocean by its characteristic brown
Sargassum seaweed and calm blue waters.
The sea is bounded on the west by the <color=#3366CC>Gulf Stream</color>, on the north by the North Atlantic Current, on the east by the
Canary Current, and on the south by the North Atlantic Equatorial Current, the four together forming a
clockwise-circulating system of ocean currents termed the North Atlantic Gyre. It lies between 20° and 35° north and
40° and 70° west and is approximately 1100 km wide by 3200 km long. <color=#3366CC>Bermuda</color> is near the western fringes of the sea.
While all of the above currents deposit marine plants and refuse into the sea, ocean water in the Sargasso Sea is
distinctive for its deep blue color and exceptional clarity, with underwater visibility of up to 60 m.
History
Portuguese navigators had reached the Sargasso Sea (western North Atlantic region), naming it after the Sargassum
seaweed growing there (sargaço or sargasso in Portuguese). Later in 1492, <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color> wrote about
seaweed that he feared would trap his ship and potentially hide shallow waters that could run them aground, as well as
a lack of wind that he feared would trap them.
The sea may have been known to earlier mariners, as a poem by 4th-century author Avienius describes a portion of the
Atlantic as being covered with seaweed and windless, citing a now-lost account by the 5th century BC <color=#3366CC>Carthaginian</color>
